sections.h2: What does selling a house in Springfield, PA involve?
sections.html:
Springfield here means Springfield Township in Delaware County, a suburb of single-family homes southwest of Philadelphia with the 19064 ZIP code. Several Pennsylvania townships share the name, so note the neighbors: Haverford, Upper Darby, Ridley, Morton, Swarthmore, Nether Providence and Marple all touch this one. Whoever buys, the sale runs through a township resale inspection, settled tax bills and a deed recorded in Media.

The township was recognized as a governmental unit in 1686 after Quakers arrived with William Penn, and it grew from farmland into a residential community once developers bought up the fields. One of the largest developments, Stoney Creek, was built between 1949 and 1954 with stone-fronted houses that were each slightly different. That postwar housing explains why many Springfield sellers are dealing with older mechanical systems and original layouts.

sections.h2: What does the Census count in Springfield's homeowner base?
sections.html:
Census estimates put the 2025 population at 25,039, nearly level with the 25,070 of 2020 and above the 24,211 of 2010. Its 6.32 square miles of land hold about 3,966 people each.

Owner occupancy is 93.8 percent, a very high rate, and 92.3 percent of people kept the same address over the past year. The middle owned home was valued at $414,900, median household income is $138,205, and households average 2.87 people. Children under 18 make up 24.2 percent of the population, so the buyers most likely to want a Springfield house are families who need space close to the city.

With so few rentals, investor-owned houses are a small part of the market. Landlords file a Business Privilege Rental Tax Return with the township, so anyone who rented the house out should ask the tax office which filings to close.

sections.h2: How does the township's resale inspection affect a Springfield sale?
sections.html:
The township homepage carries a Resale Inspection Appointment Request, which signals that a sale triggers an inspection by the code office. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, and ask what the inspector will check and how long a certificate stays valid.

The code office posts the violations it sees most often, and they double as a checklist before you list:

  • Grass cannot grow higher than 8 inches.
  • Plantings at an intersection can be no taller than 18 inches, and shrubs cannot block signs or signals.
  • House numbers must be 4 inches high and visible from the street.
  • Vehicles may park only on paved surfaces, never on the lawn.
  • Owners must maintain the curbs and sidewalks in front of the property, and snow has to come off public sidewalks within 24 hours after it stops falling.
  • Trash containers stay behind the front building line and come off the street within 12 hours of pickup.

Apply for repair permits on the township's OpenGov portal and call the inspector with questions. Large repairs are easier to defend when the paperwork exists.

sections.h2: When are Springfield township and school taxes due, and who gets paid at closing?
sections.html:
Two bills arrive each year on separate calendars, and whatever is still owed gets paid from your proceeds at closing. The township publishes both schedules.

Refuse and sewer rent ride on the township bill, with sewer rent figured from last year's water use. A sewer or refuse balance that stays unpaid becomes a lien, and real estate tax still unpaid is returned to the Tax Claim Bureau in Media by the next January. The township tax office is at 610-544-1300.

Homestead-approved properties may pay school tax in three installments, and the township's collection books close on December 31. Get the exact balance on your parcel from the tax office before settlement.

sections.h2: How much does Delaware County charge in transfer tax at recording?
sections.html:
Delaware County charges 2 percent on a transfer: one point for the state and one for the municipality. The county names four higher-rate exceptions, Radnor, Upper Darby, Upper Providence and Chester City, and Springfield is absent from that list.

Using the township's $414,900 middle value, 2 percent comes to $8,298. The contract decides who pays it, though the state holds buyer and seller jointly liable, so a title company normally collects it at the table.

Recording happens at Government Center, Room 108, 201 W. Front Street, Media; call 610-891-4152. Staff there cannot draft a deed or run a title search, and mortgages are the only liens on file with them. After a payoff the lender files a mortgage satisfaction, and the county's public access site lets you confirm your own records.

sections.h2: What shapes buyer interest in Springfield beyond the house itself?
sections.html:
Buyers look at the schools, the commute and the parks. Springfield School District serves the township with the Springfield Literacy Center for kindergarten and first grade, Scenic Hills and Harvey C. Sabold for grades 2 through 5, E. T. Richardson Middle School for grades 6 through 8, and Springfield High School, whose new building opened in 2021.

  • Roads: I-476 touches the western edge, U.S. 1 follows State Road through the north, and Pennsylvania routes 320 and 420 cross the township. The township counts 84.34 miles of public roads.
  • Transit: SEPTA's Media-Sharon Hill light rail line serves the township, SEPTA suburban buses run routes 107, 109, 110 and 111, and Regional Rail stops at nearby Swarthmore and Morton. Commutes average 27.7 minutes.
  • Retail: Baltimore Pike, nicknamed the Golden Mile, was once known for car dealerships, and Springfield Mall has about 590,000 square feet. Census figures show 2022 retail sales of $1,289,004,000.
  • Parks: there are 24 parks, including Veterans Memorial Park and Williams Park.

Darby Creek forms the northeast border and Crum Creek the west. Winters average about 33 degrees in January and July averages near 78, a humid subtropical pattern. Expect buyers to ask about water in the basement.

sections.h2: What are the practical choices if you need to sell a Springfield house quickly?
sections.html:
Listing with an agent works for a house in good shape, and clearing the violations above before it goes live keeps the resale inspection from delaying closing.

When the house needs work or the calendar is tight, selling straight to an investor or cash buyer drops lender approval and most repair haggling. Whatever you choose, get the price, closing date and transfer tax responsibility in writing, then weigh it against the net a listing would leave after fees and repairs.

faqs.q: Which county records a Springfield, PA deed?
faqs.a: Delaware County. The Recorder of Deeds is in the Government Center in Media. It records deeds and mortgages and returns the originals according to the filer's instructions, usually through the closing agent.

faqs.q: What transfer tax would a Springfield sale carry?
faqs.a: Two percent, split evenly between the state and the municipality. Springfield is not on the county's higher-rate list, so a $414,900 sale would carry $8,298.

faqs.q: Do I need a resale inspection to sell in Springfield Township?
faqs.a: The township offers a Resale Inspection Appointment Request on its homepage, so plan on one. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, to learn the current checklist and fees before you list.

faqs.q: When is the Springfield school tax discount?
faqs.a: School bills go out July 1. A 2 percent discount applies through August 31, the face amount is due from September 1 to October 31, and a 10 percent penalty starts November 1.

faqs.q: What happens to unpaid sewer and refuse charges when I sell?
faqs.a: They are filed as liens against the property, so they must be cleared. Ask the township tax office for the balance owed so the title company can pay it from your proceeds.
